findings.claim: KC[1] 'What type of battery can be charged, discharged and charged again many times?' offers 'Lead-acid battery' as a distractor and keys only 'Rechargeable (lithium-ion) battery' (correct=2) as right.
findings.truth: Lead-acid batteries are rechargeable - a car starter battery is recharged by the alternator every journey. The question therefore has two correct answers and marks a true answer wrong. Replace the distractor with a genuinely single-use cell (silver oxide button cell), which keeps the keyed index at 2.
findings.evidence: Settled battery chemistry; the lesson's own glossary defines a rechargeable battery as one 'that can be charged, discharged and charged again many times', which lead-acid satisfies.

findings.claim: KC[2] 'A cam and follower converts _____ motion into reciprocating motion.' offers 'Circular' as a distractor and keys 'Rotary' (correct=2).
findings.truth: The lesson's own key fact states 'rotary (circular)', so 'Circular' names the same motion as the keyed answer and is marked wrong. Swap the distractor for 'Reciprocating', which is one of the four spec motions and is clearly wrong in this stem.
findings.evidence: L5 content_html key fact 'The four types of motion are linear (straight line), rotary (circular), reciprocating (back-and-forth in a line) and oscillating (swinging arc)'; spec 3.1.5 names the same four motions.

findings.claim: 'the invention of graphene leading to new ultra-strong, lightweight products'
findings.truth: Graphene was isolated from graphite in 2004 by Geim and Novoselov - a discovery and an isolation process, not an invention. The point about technology push still stands, and spec 3.1.3 itself frames modern materials as coming from 'the invention of new or improved processes', so no marks turn on the wording.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.3 wording; settled history of graphene isolation

findings.claim: 'nanomaterials - materials engineered at the atomic scale to achieve enhanced properties'
findings.truth: Nanomaterials are engineered at the nanoscale, roughly 1 to 100 nanometres, which is larger than the atomic scale. The lesson's own <dfn> gives the correct definition ('billionths of a metre'), so the prose is loose rather than wrong and nothing examinable depends on it.
findings.evidence: the lesson's own data-def attribute; spec 3.1.3 lists nanomaterials without a size claim

findings.claim: 'Temperature sensors (thermistors) detect temperature changes. Their resistance decreases as temperature rises.' - repeated in KC[3] and the glossary.
findings.truth: This is true of NTC thermistors only; PTC thermistors increase in resistance as they warm. NTC is the type taught and used in GCSE D&T systems work, so the statement matches board teaching material and needs no edit.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.4 lists 'temperature sensors' without specifying the coefficient; standard GCSE D&T teaching

findings.claim: 'Use the correct technical vocabulary - "reciprocating" not "up and down", "fulcrum" not "pivot point".'
findings.truth: 'Pivot' is standard, accepted vocabulary for the fixed point of a lever, so the tip overstates the case. A student who follows the advice and writes 'fulcrum' loses nothing, so the risk is one-way and an edit is not warranted.
findings.evidence: spec 3.1.5 'Changing magnitude and direction of force'; common D&T usage of pivot and fulcrum as interchangeable

summary: Six lessons checked against AQA Design and Technology 8552 section 3.1. The technical content is sound: lever orders, cam and follower, gear ratio (60:20 = 3:1, driven three times slower with three times the torque), pulley belt directions, ferrous/non-ferrous, thermoforming/thermosetting, smart versus modern material classification and the physical/working property split all match the spec, and both Section A exam claims (1-2 mark multiple choice and short answer) are accurate. Two multiple-choice items carry a second correct answer in the distractor list and are fixed; four low-severity wording points are recorded only.
